## Introduction

Null-hypothesis significance testing (NHST), most often in the form of ANOVA and its relatives, remains the default inferential tool for treatment-effect questions in ecology and marine biology. I argue here that it is the wrong default, for reasons that hold regardless of the particular study, and I propose a replacement built from two components already well established individually — explicit causal graphs and Bayesian estimation — but rarely paired as a single, general-purpose workflow.

The case against NHST as a default does not require any particular dataset to make. A $p$-value is a statement about how surprising the observed data would be if an effect were exactly zero; it is not, and cannot be converted into, a statement about how large an effect is or how confident one should be in that size. Two effects of very different practical importance can both clear, or both fail to clear, the same significance threshold. Failing to reject a null licenses no conclusion about that null — least of all the conclusion, routinely drawn in practice, that no effect exists — because failure to reject is equally consistent with a genuine null and with an underpowered test of a real effect. And when significance testing is applied, as it typically is, to a summary outcome (a count, a biomass, a survival rate) rather than to the mechanism that generates that outcome, a significant or non-significant result cannot say which of several possible mechanisms is responsible, only that the outcome moved or did not.

These are not abstract concerns; each has been documented empirically, including within ecology and marine science specifically. @fidler2006 tracked statistical reporting practice in conservation biology across more than a decade of published articles and found that the specific error of treating a non-significant result as evidence of "no effect" did not decline as methodological criticism of NHST grew, but increased, from 47% of applicable articles in 2000–2001 to 63% in 2005. The criticism was heard; the practice worsened anyway. @qian2009 compared a Bayesian hierarchical model against conventional ANOVA on the same marine dataset — the effect of bottom-water hypoxia on Gulf of Mexico macrobenthic communities — and found the Bayesian approach both more sensitive to a real treatment effect and free of assumptions (normality, independence, balanced design) that ANOVA requires and that observational marine field data routinely violate; they advocate Bayesian hierarchical modeling as the more defensible default for this class of problem. @smith2020  makes a narrower but directly actionable recommendation: report the size of an effect and its uncertainty as the primary result, and stop using a significance threshold as a stand-in for that report.

The replacement I propose pairs two things. First, it starts from a causal graph, drawn before any statistical model is written, that states explicitly causal parentage (what is assumed to cause what), which variables are set by the experimenter versus merely observed, and which paths between a treatment and an outcome are open or blocked. Second, it fits a Bayesian generative model, consistent with that graph, that returns a full posterior distribution over the causal graph's quantities of interest rather than a binary decision about a point null.

One risk in replacing a threshold-based method with an interval-based one is reproducing the same error under a new name: treating whichever interval is reported as a discovery criterion rather than as a communication device. Nothing that follows should be read that way. The probability mass used to summarize a posterior in this paper, 94%, is a convention chosen for legibility, not a boundary the world respects; a narrower interval does not make an effect more real, and a wider one does not make it less [e.g. @mcelreath2020]. Nor does an interval replace the posterior it summarizes — it is offered because the full distribution is unwieldy to state in prose, not because inference stops at its edges. This raises a natural question: why summarize at less than 100% at all, rather than report the whole posterior as a single interval and avoid choosing a mass? For a continuous posterior this option does not exist in any useful sense. Density is nonzero arbitrarily close to every value the distribution can take, so a literal 100% interval must include the entire support — unbounded, for a parameter modeled on the log or logit scale, as every parameter in this paper is, or equal to the full legal range of the parameter even where that range is finite. Either way, a 100% interval says nothing about where probability concentrates, which is the only reason to report an interval instead of the raw posterior draws. Choosing some mass below 100% is accordingly not a matter of habit; it is the minimum commitment an interval needs to communicate anything, and the specific value chosen — 94% here, rather than the 95% NHST canonized — is a choice, defensible on grounds of convention and legibility, and reported as exactly that rather than as a discovery threshold in different clothing.

The combination is deliberately general: the same workflow — draw the graph, write the generative model, elicit priors, check the model, report contrasts as posterior distributions — applies whether the data come from a controlled experiment or from observational field data. What changes between the two is only the identification analysis the graph demands [@pearl2019]. In a controlled experiment, treatment variables are set by the experimenter, so the graph has no incoming arrows into them and no backdoor paths to close: a causal reading of the fitted contrasts follows directly from the design. In an observational study, the same graph must instead be interrogated for backdoor paths — unmeasured confounders affecting both a treatment-like variable and the outcome — and the statistical model must adjust for whatever the graph identifies as necessary, or the effect must be reported as non-identified if it does not. This paper addresses the first case, controlled experiments, in full; a subsequent paper will address the observational case using the same graph-first workflow.

@nandini2026 provides a concrete, well-documented illustration of what the controlled-experiment case looks like when analyzed the conventional way, and of exactly the failure mode described above. The study measured the functional response of the invasive hydroid *Cordylophora caspia* feeding on three zooplankton prey across three salinities, using a two-way ANOVA on prey numbers and, separately, on prey biomass consumed. Salinity and the prey$\times$salinity interaction are both significant in the numbers-consumed analysis (salinity: $F_{2,27}=3.78$, $p=0.036$; interaction: $F_{4,27}=3.57$, $p=0.018$), while neither is significant for biomass (salinity: $p=0.256$; interaction: $p=0.650$). The paper's stated conclusion — that salinity had no effect on feeding behavior across the tested range — is accurate for biomass but not for numbers, and a reader relying on the summary conclusion would not know a significant result exists in the paper's own results table. Nothing about the experimental design is at fault here; the treatment variables (prey identity, salinity, offered density) are fully under experimental control, which is exactly the setting in which the workflow proposed above requires no adjustment step and should be most straightforward to apply. What is at fault is the inferential layer: two separate significance tests on two related outcomes, with no shared generative model connecting them, no effect size reported with its uncertainty, and no mechanism-level quantity (only raw counts and biomass) available to explain why prey identity or salinity might matter.

The remainder of this paper reanalyzes the Nandini et al. dataset under the proposed workflow: a causal graph specific to this experiment, a Bayesian generative model of the underlying Holling functional response consistent with that graph, and posterior contrasts — reported as effect sizes with uncertainty rather than as significance decisions — on the same questions the original ANOVA addressed.
